title: Microsoft Foundry: publish agents to the Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Store without code
summary: Hold: the briefing overstates what blocking a Foundry agent accomplishes. Microsoft says this admin-centre action affects Foundry agents only in Copilot Chat, so administrators must not rely on it to stop access in Teams.

claims.claim: The roadmap describes direct no-code publishing of Azure AI Foundry agents to the Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Store.
claims.quote: Developers can now publish Azure AI Foundry Agents directly to the Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Store with a simplified, no-code experience.

claims.claim: Developers can publish from the Foundry portal to Microsoft Copilot and Teams without manually building a separate app package.
claims.quote: Publishing from the portal calls Foundry's Microsoft 365 publish API and builds the Teams app package for you.

claims.claim: The feature's Learn page uses the product name Microsoft Foundry.
claims.quote: When you publish a Microsoft Foundry agent to Microsoft Copilot and Teams, you and others can interact with and discover your agent through the Microsoft Copilot and Teams UI.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Data exposure; rationale: risk
claims.claim: Microsoft 365 and Teams process and store data associated with publishing and using the agent.
claims.quote: When you publish agents to Microsoft 365 and Teams, those services process and store certain data associated with publishing and using the agent.

claims.claim: That data includes publishing metadata such as name, icon and description, and data in responses to users' queries.
claims.quote: This data can include data necessary to publish the agent, such as the agent's name, icon, and description. It also includes data contained in responses provided by the agent when users in your organization submit queries to the agent from Microsoft 365 and Teams.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Data exposure; Governance guidance
claims.claim: Microsoft 365 and Teams terms and commitments apply to this data and Microsoft advises evaluating compliance and residency before publication.
claims.quote: This data is subject to the terms, compliance commitments, data residency commitments, and data handling practices applicable to Microsoft 365 and Teams.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Data exposure; Governance guidance
claims.claim: Microsoft warns not to include secrets, API keys or sensitive information in user-visible metadata.
claims.quote: Don't include secrets, API keys, or sensitive information in any metadata fields. These fields are visible to users.

claims.quote: Publishing from the Foundry portal isn't supported for projects that disable public network access. To publish these agents, use the REST API and enable the source-IP-filtered public Activity Protocol route with `enable_m365_public_endpoint`.

claims.where: front matter: licensing.model and cost; Cost and licensing; rationale: cost
claims.claim: Consumption is the documented Foundry billing model relevant to running the agent, with separate model, tool and resource meters.
claims.quote: When an agent in Foundry Agent Service runs, you pay for the model calls it makes and for the tools and resources it uses. Each item bills on its own meters, so an agent's total cost spans several meters in Azure Cost Management.
claims.fix: Keep the Azure-meter statement, but add: 'The Agent Applications FAQ describes published applications as publisher-pays, with costs based on deployed underlying infrastructure rather than per-call consumption: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/agent-applications#faqs.' This is a different emphasis in Microsoft's published-agent billing guidance, not grounds to discard the cited billing page.

claims.claim: Foundry charges are Azure costs borne by the publisher's project infrastructure rather than charges owned by the Microsoft 365 admin centre.
claims.quote: Published agents use a publisher-pays model: the publisher (the Foundry project owner) incurs costs based on the underlying infrastructure that is deployed when the agent is published as an application, not based on per-call consumption.
claims.fix: Add https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/agent-applications#faqs to sources for the publisher-pays attribution.

claims.claim: The portal publishing prerequisites include portal access, a project with a tested agent version and Foundry User at project scope, and name no Microsoft 365 licence.
claims.quote: Access to the [Microsoft Foundry portal] ... A [Foundry project] with an agent version you tested and want to publish ... **Foundry User** role on the Foundry project scope to create, manage, and publish agents.

claims.claim: Microsoft Learn publishes no separate charge or meter specifically for publishing an agent to the Agent Store.
claims.quote: Searched: Foundry publish agent Microsoft 365 Copilot publishing pricing meter license; Microsoft Foundry publish Agent Store publishing charge pricing. Opened publish-copilot and billing-concepts; read Agent Applications FAQ. Results describe runtime/infrastructure costs, not a Store publishing meter.
